overview: The Federal Protective Service, part of the Department of Homeland Security, guards many federal office buildings around the country. This bill directs it, within one year, to create and put in place guidance on how to quickly warn federal workers in those buildings about violent threats inside or within about 150 feet of the building, such as shootings, weapons threats, terrorism, or suspicious packages, and how to tell them what to do to stay safe. A designated security official at each building would be responsible for carrying out the guidance, and the agency would have to run periodic drills to test readiness. The agency must also send Congress a short report and briefing on the practices it adopts. No new money is provided. The Senate passed it on August 7, 2026, and as of August 10, 2026, it was being held at the desk in the House.
for: Supporters say federal employees deserve clear, timely alerts during an emergency, and that consistent procedures across buildings could save lives when a threat occurs.
against: Critics say requiring new protocols, drills and reports without any added funding could stretch the agency's existing security resources thin.
